title: How To Make Dhaniya Panjiri for Janmashtami in Under 15 Minutes
excerpt: This traditional coriander-based prasad, made with ghee, dry fruits, and roasted spices, is one of the simplest and most beloved offerings for Lord Krishna's birthday.
body:
• Dhaniya panjiri, made from roasted coriander seeds, ghee, dry fruits, and sugar, is a traditional Janmashtami prasad offered to Lord Krishna across North Indian households
  • The recipe takes just 10-15 minutes to prepare and requires no cooking expertise — dry-roasting and grinding are the only techniques involved
  • Key ingredients include coriander seeds, makhana (lotus seeds), almonds, cashews, melon seeds, grated coconut, cardamom, and ghee
  • Janmashtami 2026 falls on September 4, making this the ideal week to prepare this festive offering

A Prasad Rooted in Devotion

As Janmashtami approaches, kitchens across India and the diaspora begin to fill with the warm, earthy fragrance of roasting coriander. Dhaniya panjiri — a crumbly, nutty mixture of ground coriander, ghee-roasted dry fruits, and powdered sugar — is among the most beloved offerings made to Lord Krishna on his birthday.

Unlike the elaborate sweets that mark many Hindu festivals, panjiri is defined by its simplicity. It requires no oven, no syrup, no complicated technique. The entire preparation comes together in a single heavy-bottomed pan, making it accessible to cooks of every skill level.

Why Coriander Takes Center Stage

Coriander seeds are considered auspicious in Hindu tradition and are closely associated with Krishna worship. When dry-roasted in ghee, the seeds release a warm, citrusy aroma that becomes the signature note of panjiri. The seeds are coarsely ground — not powdered into oblivion — so the finished prasad retains a pleasant, granular texture that distinguishes it from finer desserts like ladoo or barfi.

The use of whole coriander also connects panjiri to Ayurvedic tradition, where the spice is valued for its digestive and cooling properties — fitting for a preparation associated with the monsoon season, when Janmashtami typically falls.

The Recipe

The preparation begins with dry-roasting half a cup of coarsely ground coriander seeds in a teaspoon of ghee over low heat. Patience is key: the coriander must turn aromatic and deepen in color without burning. Once done, it is transferred to a plate to cool completely.

In the same pan, makhana (lotus seeds) are roasted in another teaspoon of ghee until they turn crunchy. These join the coriander on the cooling plate. Next, two teaspoons of ghee go into the pan for the dry fruits: chopped almonds, cashews, chironji, melon seeds, and raisins are stirred until golden. Grated dry coconut is added last and roasted gently.

Once all the roasted components have cooled, they are combined in a mixing bowl with powdered sugar (or boora, a traditional coarse sugar), cardamom powder, and a few tulsi leaves. The mixture is crumbled together by hand until everything is evenly distributed.

The result is a fragrant, crumbly prasad that balances the warmth of roasted coriander with the richness of ghee-toasted nuts and the gentle sweetness of sugar.

Variations Across Regions

While the core recipe remains consistent across North India, regional variations exist. Some households add gondh (edible gum), which is deep-fried in ghee until it puffs up before being mixed in. Others incorporate dried rose petals for fragrance or fennel seed powder for an added layer of flavor. In parts of Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, families use desi khand — an unrefined granulated sugar — instead of boora, lending a slightly deeper, molasses-adjacent sweetness.

For the Diaspora Kitchen

For Indian families abroad, panjiri is one of the easiest festive preparations to replicate. Coriander seeds, ghee, and most dry fruits are available at any Indian grocery store, and the recipe requires no specialized equipment. Many families prepare a larger batch and store it in airtight containers, sharing portions with friends and neighbors as Janmashtami prasad.

"The two most important ingredients in panjiri are patience with the roasting and good-quality ghee. Everything else follows."

— Chef Aarti Madan, food creator

Serving and Storage

Panjiri is traditionally offered as bhog alongside makhan mishri (butter with crystallized sugar), fresh fruits, and panchamrit — a mixture of milk, curd, honey, ghee, and sugar. After the offering and aarti, it is distributed among family and visitors as prasad.

Stored in an airtight container at room temperature, panjiri stays fresh for up to two weeks, making it a practical choice for families who want to prepare ahead of the festival.
